title: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
description: The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene
body: The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene for signs of hypothermia. A small craft was then deployed which - along with "land-based units" from the local fire and rescue service - conducted "a thorough sweep of the area but found no one in the water"."Following the operation, at approximately 08:00 (09:00 GMT) the body of a man in his twenties was discovered on the beach," the coastguard reported. It adds an investigation will be opened to "determine the circumstances surrounding the incident".In the latest week of data, ending 8 November, the UK government reported that 903 migrants arrived by small boat into the UK in 14 boats. A further 624 migrants were prevented from making the crossing, the data shows. Earlier this year, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review after two boats carrying 21 people landed in Kent without being intercepted. "Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many," she said at the time.

schema.headline: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing

title: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
description: King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th bir
body: King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts. "We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary."I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said."I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others.Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano.The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful". Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee."I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said."It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message."

schema.headline: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
description: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volody
body: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance to deter future threats, but this previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas."The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the the Kherson region to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

schema.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

title: Andy Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister
description: The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown ou
body: The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.On Saturday morning Andy Burnham addressed the first Welsh Labour conference since May's Senedd election.He suggested the previous Labour government did not do enough to pass powers down to communities, and said it was "hard" to accept the party was no longer in power after 27 years of running the Welsh government.He spoke before a review into what went wrong concluded that former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy of calling out Westminster played a role in the party losing power.Prof Anand Menon, of PF Global, said Morgan's calls for constitutional change like the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate did not get through to voters.Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party for focusing too much on powers for the Senedd.In a subdued speech, Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" where "everyone" was "signed up and on the same page."He spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election.Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils."Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place."We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places."He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom."Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction"."Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve."We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice."Addressing the event at Venue Cymru in Llandudno, Burnham said he loved "everything about Wales".He said his last visit to Wales - to Aberfan - left the "biggest mark" of his visits to the country.Referencing the fight for justice in the years after the disaster, Burnham said he wanted a "country where all people and all places are treated fairly and with dignity".He said his vision for the country is a "reindustrialised nation with revitalised high streets".Burnham said Labour should be "immensely proud" of the things it achieved in Wales - including free school meals, free prescription and the creation of Transport for Wales.The prime minister said he wanted to show how "being in the UK is good for Wales because of the partnership that we can develop together".Burnham said he had put the full devolution of employment support on the table with the Welsh government.It was announced at the Budget that standing charges for gas will come to an end. Burnham confirmed that the charges will be scrapped in the new year.Menon's criticism of Red Welsh Way was one of several findings, including that the party suffered a long-term decline in support, laid bare as Labour took flak for dissatisfaction with public services.It said "weaknesses in political communication" also left the party without "clear answers when voters wanted them.The review says Labour should set itself against Plaid Cymru's "constitutional project", by seeking more powers based on what they would deliver rather than "debating powers in the abstract".Labour has shared most of Plaid's constitutional demands, including the devolution of policing, the Crown Estate and rail devolution, with the exception of independence.Plaid beat Welsh Labour in the May election, and was now running the Welsh government.Morgan sought to differentiate herself from Sir Keir Starmer with a flagship speech in 2025, where she set out her approach called the Red Welsh Way.Morgan said she was willing to "call out" Westminster Labour, and demanded the devolution of the crown estate to the Senedd.Menon's report said the policy "struggled to land on everyday policy, instead tied up in constitutional positioning and the relationship with Westminster"."Demands such as transferring the Crown Estate and devolving policing did not speak to voters on the doorstep, who found themselves more concerned with the economy, cost of living and the NHS."He said the Labour campaign shifted from Red Welsh Way to "power in partnership" - attempting to send signals about the relationship with UK Labour in government, "but still did not provide clear policy objectives, whether in terms of common ground or differentiation".The report said Welsh Labour "should define standing up for Wales by what it delivers on the issues voters care about most: the NHS, the cost of living and the economy.It calls for Labour to seek further powers for the Senedd and within Wales "where they would improve delivery or bring decisions closer to people."Menon said the result was "not necessarily" about Welsh identity, saying Welsh identity "has been flat for a decade".But he added: "Welsh Labour voters who switch to Plaid do score more strongly on their Welsh identity than those who stayed."Focus group participants also cited it as a reason for switching, objecting to 'the lack of Labour standing up for Wales as a separate entity'."However, voters tend to judge whether a party stands up for Wales mainly on delivery: the NHS, the cost of living and the economy. "For the median Welsh voter, identity operates through these issues more than through a clear demand for further devolution, independence or a focus on the Welsh language."

schema.headline: Andy Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister

title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
description: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform t
body: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process."I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.  In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December."It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says."I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

schema.headline: I took Vinted to court to get my money back

title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
description: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable femal
body: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D gamesByLaura CressTechnology reporterAfter a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment."We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.Image caption, Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft AutoThe original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table."At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, DMA Design / BMG InteractiveImage caption, The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2DSlide 1 of 7, A screenshot from the original Grand Theft Auto. The words BUSTED! is shown in yellow. A top down view shows several police cars with sirens on and a red car with door open, and a person on the road., The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D'More fun' playing the bad guyThe team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer. But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book"."At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it"."For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow."And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that  was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt."We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald."It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA."It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says."Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's mapWhen GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming."I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life"."It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."Image caption, "It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, leftGTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game."Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald. "It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time."It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says."But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful"."It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."Get in touchAre you a fan of the game? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6

title: Keaton Slater's parents' fight to bring Latvian killer to UK
description: Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to
body: Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.This article contains upsetting detailsDolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.The car did not stop.As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.Taiwo Owatemi, MP for Coventry North West, was working behind the scenes to build political support.Colleagues in Westminster had warned her that, without an extradition agreement between the UK and EU, securing Dolars' return would be extremely difficult.However, she was encouraged by the Latvian ambassador telling her his country did not want a difficult relationship with the UK, given the proximity of the country to Ukraine and its continuing war with Russia.She also learned from him that Latvians were angry at what had happened and that  Dolars was bringing shame on their country."When you have Latvians in Latvia asking for justice, when you have Latvians in the UK asking for justice, that's his number one job as ambassador," Owatemi said.Latvians were also proactive identifying where Dolars was in the country, she said.Louise said she had received messages from families there via a Facebook page set up within the community after Keaton's death.She said people were saying, "we don't want him here, he's scum".They also sent a video of Dolars happily walking around and also with his car. She sent them to police."He was free. He thought he'd got away with it," she said.In February 2026, there was a breakthrough. The Latvian government considered legislation to allow citizens to be extradited to the UK for prosecution.Campaigning by the family had helped bring about a new law where instances of extradition would now be considered on a case-by-case basis.

schema.headline: Keaton Slater's parents' fight to bring Latvian killer to UK

title: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?
description: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner p
body: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate. Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between. Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK."It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job". So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."The most popular Christmas trees available in the UK are the Nordmann fir variety, which are non-drop, meaning they don't drop their needles. Norway Spruce is another common variety and have a strong pine scent, but generally should be kept outdoors or put up just before Christmas.Pine trees, Walker says, have the longest lifespan, but he concedes they lack that classic Christmas look.Or, of course, you could opt for a tried-and-tested artificial tree, which is what Katie McDonald from Belfast put up in her house last week."When I was a kid my mum always waited to the last minute to let us kids put the tree up. We would be the last house on our street and the last of all our friends to get the tree up," she tells the BBC."So I made myself a wee childlike promise that when I had my own house I'd be one of the first to put my tree up."She says she will replace her artificial tree with a real one in a few weeks, so it is in prime condition come Christmas Day.

schema.headline: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?

title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The histori
body: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters."The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment.No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025."President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September. Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says

title: Sandpaper scandal: David Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'
description: David Warner has accused Cricket Australia (CA) of a "cover up" as the row over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continued.Former vice-captain Warner,
body: David Warner has accused Cricket Australia (CA) of a "cover up" as the row over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continued.Former vice-captain Warner, captain Steve Smith and opener Cameron Bancroft all served lengthy bans as part of CA's investigation into the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket during a Test series in South Africa in 2018. Batter Usman Khawaja has reopened discussions about the scandal with explosive claims in his new autobiography, where he said the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball. And Warner has questioned the investigation into the incident by claiming that Australia's bowlers from the Cape Town Test were not interviewed. "As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said."If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know? "It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. "That stinks of a cover-up."The four frontline bowlers - Hazlewood, Starc, Lyon and Pat Cummins - have maintained they did not know about the plan to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball.Cummins, Australia's Test captain since 2021, said in his extraordinary news conference on Friday that he was interviewed as part of the investigation.In response to Warner's comments, CA said: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since."Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players' right to provide their own version of events."

schema.headline: Sandpaper scandal: David Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'

title: Bletchley Park officer's Aston Martin DB5 to be sold at auction
description: An Aston Martin car owned by a British intelligence officer, and of the same model made famous by the James Bond films, is expected to fetch up to £40
body: An Aston Martin car owned by a British intelligence officer, and of the same model made famous by the James Bond films, is expected to fetch up to £400,000 when it goes to auction.The red Aston Martin DB5 Sports Saloon car will go on sale at Sandown Park in Esher, Surrey.It was owned by PH Manners Wood, who interpreted decoded enigma messages at Bletchley Park during World War Two, and who bought the car in the same year Bond first hit the big screen.Paul Cheetham, of auctioneers H&H Classics, said: "James Bond was not the only British intelligence officer to take delivery of an Aston Martin DB5 during 1964, as seen with this wonderful example first owned by Manners Wood."He added that the car had "links to a real British hero who, along with his colleagues, made such a difference to help end the hostilities in the Second World War".The Aston Martin DB5 has also become synonymous with the Bond films thanks to its use in movies such as Goldfinger alongside Sean Connery, and Skyfall with Daniel Craig's 007.The next James Bond film is currently reported to be casting its new lead, with speculation as to which actor will take up the mantle.Manners Wood's rare DB5 is among just under 900 of the cars to be produced and has had two owners since, including its current owner who has looked after it for 56 years, according to H&H Classics.The intelligence officer worked at Bletchley Park and was credited with saving thousands of lives by General Dwight D Eisenhower, later to become US president.H&H Classics says the DB5 will go on display at Sandown Park on 9 December, ahead of the auction the following day.Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Bletchley Park officer's Aston Martin DB5 to be sold at auction

title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
description: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".It comes after ITV News an
body: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s"."Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened."We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with."I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. "And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

schema.headline: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences

title: Thomas Tuchel: England boss to remind players of anti-racism protocols before Spain game
description: Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.The
body: Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt."We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place. "Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system. Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field. If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned."It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said."And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

schema.headline: Thomas Tuchel: England boss to remind players of anti-racism protocols before Spain game

title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
description: Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the B
body: Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.He claims the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it spends on supporting them into employment, and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - £25 to one, and we can take everything to £2 to one".He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.Milburn said the government is already spending £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive, and that money needs to be spent differently. He has already said that the under 25s should no longer be able to claim some health benefits – the personal independence payment and the health element of Universal Credit.In his other major announcement, Milburn spoke of the proposal he calls an "opportunity guarantee" for young people.This would put a legal duty on government to ensure young people have access to a route into employment.He said: "It should be a guarantee for a young person. Because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is a very simple thing. To get a benefit. What sort of life is that?"The "opportunity guarantee" might work similarly to the way that councils have a legal responsibility to offer homeless people accommodation or advice, or accommodate children in care.Milburn argues previous employment schemes have been temporary, and says a permanent legal entitlement is needed to tackle the long-running problem of young people not in education, employment or training.The government is expected broadly to welcome the proposals, which will be published in full on Tuesday, with a statement in Parliament and draft laws early next year.Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training - otherwise known as Neet - according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic. "It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning. Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away. "It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said."A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

schema.headline: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
